I started using Linux in 95, and in the group of tech people i got to know (through various LAN parties etc) Slackware was/is to learn Linux to the core, the hardcore way. Things needed to be configured directly in files, you compiled your own builds and it generally is a more manual system. The slackware philosophy is to be the most UNIX-like Linux distro. UNIX being the system Linux is based on but it was very expensive to buy, so some people got together to make a free open source alternative and when Linux Torvalds made the kernel for free and gave it to the public under GPL license it got really popular.

Now a days though Slackware does have a package system which saves a lot of work. I havent used . since version 12 so people have to correct me if im wrong but slackware still is a bit of a manual system, forcing you to really get in to the nuts and bolts of Linux.

Slackware is wonderful. The commentary contained in config files (under /etc for example) is invaluable. Everything is in the right place too. When you grab a source tarball and read the README or INSTALL you know that things will go according to plan. I never had that experience with any other distribution. Slackware has things where they should be. Makes life easier.

well one of the main things you can do is delete temporary files that are in prefetch and %temp% (run).
